title: Cap. IX Corvini Arg. 1: as God damns the gospel-contumacious in time, so he reprobated them from eternity
latin: Cap. IX. Corvini argumenta proponuntur et diluuntur. Argumentari igitur solent adversarii ab ipso damnandi decreto ad actum sive decretum reprobationis, hoc modo: Qualiter consideratos Deus damnat in tempore, taliter consideratos decrevit damnare, et reprobavit ab aeterno. Sed damnat homines consideratos ut Evangelio immorigeros, hoc est, ut finaliter impenitentes et incredulos: Ergo etiam taliter consideratos reprobavit.
pass_a: Chapter IX. The arguments of Corvinus are proposed and dissolved. The adversaries therefore are wont to argue from the very decree of damning unto the act or decree of reprobation, in this manner: In what manner considered God damns in time, in such manner considered he decreed to damn, and reprobated from eternity. But he damns men considered as contumacious unto the Gospel, that is, as finally impenitent and unbelieving: Therefore he also reprobated them so considered.
pass_b: Chapter IX — Corvinus's arguments proposed and dissolved. Adversaries commonly argue from the decree of damning to the act or decree of reprobation thus: In whatever manner of consideration God damns in time, in that same manner he decreed to damn and reprobated from eternity. But he damns men considered as contumacious to the Gospel — that is, as finally impenitent and unbelieving. Therefore he also reprobated them so considered.

lemmas.gloss: from damning decree to reprobation act

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1: major — sin's relation to damnation same as to reprobation; wisdom would not reprobate without demerit
latin: Majorem inde liquere putant, quod quam rationem peccatum habet ad damnationem, eandem etiam habeat ad reprobationem: atque idcirco sicuti agnoscitur habere rationem causae meritoriae et moventis ipsum Deum ad damnationem hujus vel illius singularis personae, ita etiam se habere debet ad reprobationem. Hisce omnibus adjiciunt, repugnare Divinae sapientiae, ut velit reprobare peccatorem sine meritorum malorum consideratione, et tamen eundem in tempore nisi propter mala merita nolit condemnare.
pass_a: They think the Major thence clear, that what reason sin has unto damnation, the same it also has unto reprobation: and therefore as it is acknowledged to have the reason of a meritorious and moving cause of God himself unto the damnation of this or that singular person, so also it ought to have itself unto reprobation. To all these they add that it repugns Divine wisdom, that he should will to reprobate a sinner without consideration of evil merits, and yet be unwilling to condemn the same in time except on account of evil merits.
pass_b: They take the Major as clear from this: whatever relation sin has to damnation, it has the same to reprobation — so as sin is granted meritorious and moving cause moving God to damn this or that particular person, it must likewise stand toward reprobation. They add that it clashes with divine wisdom to will to reprobate a sinner without regard to evil merits, yet refuse to condemn him in time except for evil merits.

lemmas.gloss: sin as meritorious moving cause of damnation
wisdom would not reprobate without demerit yet damn for it

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: head of error — reprobation is not the same as the decree of damning
latin: In causa praedestinationis consimili argumento utuntur tum Jesuitae tum Arminiani, cui a nobis antea satisfactum fuit. In hoc argumento caput erroris est, quod reprobatio sive decretum reprobandi idem prorsus esse praesumitur, quod decretum damnandi. Nobis autem decretum damnandi designat sententiam peremptoriam in mente Dei Judicis ab aeterno conceptam, et voluntatis placito confirmatam, qua hominem praevisum et consideratum, ut peccati in ipso exitu hujus vitae reum, statuit propter illud peccatum aeterna morte punire: decretum autem reprobandi denotat aeternum placitum Dei, non ut Judicis, sed ut liberrimi Agentis, quo apud se statuit quibusdam personis non apponere illam specialis et indebitae misericordiae gratiam, quae de facto eos emolliret, converteret et ad vitam aeternam perduceret.
pass_a: In the cause of predestination Jesuits and Arminians alike use a like argument, to which satisfaction was given by us before. In this argument the head of the error is, that reprobation or the decree of reprobating is presumed to be altogether the same as the decree of damning. But to us the decree of damning designates a peremptory sentence conceived from eternity in the mind of God the Judge, and confirmed by the good pleasure of the will, by which he established to punish with eternal death, on account of that sin, a man foresighted and considered as guilty of sin in the very exit of this life: but the decree of reprobating denotes the eternal good pleasure of God, not as Judge, but as freest Agent, by which he established with himself not to apply to certain persons that grace of special and unowed mercy which in fact would soften them, convert them, and lead them unto eternal life.
pass_b: Jesuits and Arminians use a like argument in the predestination debate — and we answered it before. The head of the error here is presuming reprobation, or the decree to reprobate, is altogether the same as the decree to damn. For us the decree to damn names a peremptory sentence conceived from eternity in the mind of God the Judge and confirmed by his will's good pleasure: to punish with eternal death, for that sin, a man foresighted and considered guilty of sin at this life's very exit. The decree to reprobate names God's eternal good pleasure not as Judge but as freest Agent: resolving not to apply to certain persons that grace of special unowed mercy which would in fact soften, convert, and lead them to eternal life.

lemmas.gloss: damning as Judge; reprobating as free Agent

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: wide difference of the two decrees; Major and its confirmation invalid
latin: Inter haec duo decreta latum discrimen est. Prius ex justitia vindicante procedit, ac proinde ad finalem reatum peccatoris, tanquam causam motivam supplicii destinati, respicit. Posterius ex libertate Dei de suo quod vult facientis egreditur, ac proinde, sicuti cum Deus statuit dare speciale beneficium alicui personae singulari, non inde sequitur, illum respexisse merita ejusdem personae, tanquam praedictae beneficentiae causam motivam, ita cum statuit non dare illud idem speciale beneficium alteri, non inde recte deducitur, illum ad finalia personae hujus demerita, tanquam ad causam motivam negatae hujus beneficentiae, respexisse. Majorem igitur propositionem, atque ejusdem confirmationem, invalidam esse dicimus, quia non est uniformis consideratio neque eadem habitudo peccati quoad decretum reprobandi, quae est ejusdem quoad decretum damnandi. Neque omnino repugnat, imo optime congruit, sapientiae Divinae, ut nolit quenquam condemnare nisi propter demeritum peccati tanquam causam antecedaneam et motivam supplicii destinati, et tamen velit aliquos reprobare (hoc est, in gratiae specialis praeparatione et infallibili ad vitam aeternam ordinatione praeterire) ex mera libertate suae voluntatis, et non ex antecedaneo infidelitatis aut impoenitentiae finalis motivo.
pass_a: Between these two decrees there is a wide discrimination. The former proceeds from vindicating justice, and therefore regards the final guilt of the sinner as the moving cause of the destined punishment. The latter goes forth from the liberty of God doing of his own what he wills, and therefore, as when God established to give a special benefit to some singular person, it does not thence follow that he regarded the merits of the same person as the moving cause of the foresaid beneficence, so when he established not to give that same special benefit to another, it is not thence rightly deduced that he regarded unto the final demerits of this person as unto the moving cause of this denied beneficence. We therefore say that the Major proposition, and the confirmation of the same, is invalid, because there is not a uniform consideration nor the same habit of sin as to the decree of reprobating which there is of the same as to the decree of damning. Nor does it altogether repugn, nay it best agrees, with Divine wisdom, that he be unwilling to condemn anyone except on account of the demerit of sin as antecedent and moving cause of the destined punishment, and yet will to reprobate certain ones (that is, to pass by in the preparation of special grace and the infallible ordination unto eternal life) from the mere liberty of his will, and not from an antecedent motive of final unbelief or impenitence.
pass_b: Between these two decrees the difference is wide. The first proceeds from vindicating justice, and so regards the sinner's final guilt as moving cause of the destined punishment. The second goes forth from God's liberty doing of his own what he wills. As when God resolves to give a special benefit to some particular person it does not follow that he regarded that person's merits as moving cause of the beneficence, so when he resolves not to give that same special benefit to another, it is not rightly deduced that he regarded that person's final demerits as moving cause of the denied beneficence. So we call the Major and its confirmation invalid: there is neither uniform consideration nor the same relation of sin to the decree of reprobating as to the decree of damning. Far from clashing with divine wisdom, it best agrees with it that God refuse to condemn anyone except for sin's demerit as antecedent moving cause of destined punishment — and yet will to reprobate some (that is, pass them by in preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life) from mere liberty of will, not from an antecedent motive of final unbelief or impenitence.

lemmas.gloss: damning from justice; reprobating from liberty
sin's habit to damning ≠ to reprobating

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: Bannes and Lombard — praeterition manifests liberty in dispensing supernatural goods
latin: Recte Bannes, Haec praeteritio sive reprobatio aliquarum personarum, aliis electis, est manifestativa maximae libertatis quam habet Divina voluntas circa dispensationem bonorum supernaturalium, In 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. pag. 293. Jam vero haud alienum est a sapientia Divina, sicuti et reliqua sua attributa, ita et hoc libertatis attributum in summo bono dispensando hominibus manifestare. Unde Lombardus, lib. 1. dist. 41, Reprobavit Deus quos voluit, non propter futura merita quae praevideret, veritate tamen rectissima, a nostris sensibus remota. Haec de Majore.
pass_a: Rightly Bannes, This passing by or reprobation of certain persons, others being elected, is manifestative of the greatest liberty which the Divine will has concerning the dispensation of supernatural goods, On 1, question 23, article 5, page 293. But now it is by no means alien from Divine wisdom, as also its other attributes, so also to manifest this attribute of liberty in dispensing the highest good unto men. Whence Lombard, book 1, distinction 41, God reprobated whom he willed, not on account of future merits which he foresaw, yet by a most right truth, removed from our senses. These things concerning the Major.
pass_b: Bannes puts it well: this praeterition or reprobation of some persons, others being elect, manifests the greatest liberty the divine will has in dispensing supernatural goods (on ST I, q. 23 a. 5, p. 293). Nor is it alien to divine wisdom — as with his other attributes — to manifest this attribute of liberty in dispensing the highest good to men. So Lombard (Sentences 1, dist. 41): God reprobated whom he willed, not for future merits he foresaw — yet by a most right truth, remote from our senses. So much for the Major.

lemmas.gloss: praeterition manifests liberty in supernatural goods
reprobated whom he willed, not for foresight merits

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp. Minor: not all damned as gospel-contumacious; reprobation's cause lies elsewhere
latin: Accedamus ad Minorem; quae non est vera, si universaliter intelligatur. Nam multi damnantur, qui ut Evangelio immorigeri minime a Deo considerantur. Exemplo sint infantes Paganorum, qui filii irae nascuntur, et in Christo minime renascuntur. Exemplo etiam esse possunt inter adultos illi omnes, quibus nec Evangelium illuxit unquam, nec Christus innotuit: Quin etiam multos per solam Legem damnari, et non propter Evangelium contemptum, concedit Arminius, Exam. Praedest. Perkins. Sed non est quod ultra laboremus de Minore. Nam sive ob contemptum Evangelii, sive ob contemptum Legis homines damnentur, tamen, quod iidem reprobentur, aliunde causam habet. Denique, damus, homines reprobari non sine consideratione spretæ Legis, aut Evangelii, quia Deus non potest aliquem reprobare, nisi ut peccati reum: sed ex praeconsideratione fidei futurae in aliquibus, et in aliis praeconsideratione peccati futuri, haud consequitur. Multa enim a Deo eligente aut reprobante praevidentur ab aeterno in electis aut reprobatis futura, quae non habent rationem causae motivae ad actum reprobandi vel eligendi.
pass_a: Let us approach the Minor; which is not true, if it be understood universally. For many are damned, who are least considered by God as contumacious unto the Gospel. Let the infants of the Pagans be an example, who are born children of wrath, and are least reborn in Christ. An example also among adults can be all those to whom neither the Gospel ever shone, nor Christ became known: Nay even that many are damned by the Law alone, and not on account of contempt of the Gospel, Arminius concedes, Examination of the Predestination of Perkins. But there is no reason that we labor further concerning the Minor. For whether men be damned on account of contempt of the Gospel, or on account of contempt of the Law, yet that the same are reprobated has its cause from elsewhere. Finally, we grant that men are reprobated not without consideration of a despised Law, or Gospel, because God cannot reprobate anyone except as guilty of sin: but from preconsideration of future faith in some, and in others preconsideration of future sin, it by no means follows. For many things are foresighted from eternity by God electing or reprobating as future in the elect or reprobate, which do not have the reason of a moving cause unto the act of reprobating or of electing.
pass_b: Now the Minor — which is not true if taken universally. Many are damned who are not at all considered by God as contumacious to the Gospel. Example: pagan infants, born children of wrath and not reborn in Christ. Among adults, all those to whom the Gospel never shone nor Christ became known. Arminius even grants that many are damned by the Law alone, not for contempt of the Gospel (Examination of Perkins's Predestination). No need to labor further on the Minor. Whether men are damned for contempt of Gospel or of Law, that the same are reprobated has its cause elsewhere. Finally we grant men are not reprobated without regard to a despised Law or Gospel, because God cannot reprobate anyone except as guilty of sin — but it does not follow from preconsideration of future faith in some and future sin in others. God electing or reprobating foresights from eternity many future things in elect and reprobate that are not moving causes of the act of electing or reprobating.

lemmas.gloss: Minor fails universally; many damned without gospel contempt
